          "text": "## 3.2.2. Metal content\nFor the finest fraction, data show a predominance of Ni (that constitutes about 64% in weight), and significant amounts of Co, Tl, Sn, Mn, Fe and K. Also the 1–3 mm fraction appeared mainly enriched in these same metals, as well as in Zn.\nThese data reflect clearly the composition of the electrodes of this type of battery. The cathode, the same used for the Ni–Cd batteries, is constituted of nickel and cobalt hydroxide. Comparing the concentration of these two metals in the fraction 1 mm < U < 3 mm of the first two kinds of batteries examined, it is possible to note a consistency: Ni / CoNi-Cd = 10 and Ni / CoNi-MH = 10.3. This means that for both kinds of batteries, in this fraction a higher concentration of cathode elements results.\nOn the other hand, negative electrode is made up mainly of nickel (high quantities in the fine fraction <1 mm) and rare earth (Pietrelli et al., 2005). This result confirms what was inferred for\nNi–Cd batteries – that the cathode tends to be reduced into finer particles, compared to the anode, during the milling process.\nPotassium derives from electrolyte, whereas iron could derive from the metallic alloys, used for the anode.\nThe values obtained agree well with other literature data (Rabah et al., 2008: Ni: 87%, Cd: 9–10%). Considering these results, it can be observed that about 630 g Ni, 78 g Co and 40 g Fe (respectively, 80%, 84% and 67% of which is in the finest fraction) could be recovered from 1 kg of mixed Ni-MH spent batteries.           "text": "## 3.4. Leaching test\nFig. 2 shows pH and conductivity results for the leaching tests. Values of pH found for leachate solutions are always basic and, in the case of Ni–Cd and Ni-MH batteries, highly basic, due to the presence of hydroxides in the electrolytes.\nThe resulting electrical conductivity (4–11 mS/cm) can be mainly ascribed to the electrolyte dissolution. Indeed, the amount of metals (as reported in Table 3, together with the other ions investigated) is rather limited, and therefore, in all samples, the size reduction and the absence of a barrier as the plastic shell, do not determine a particular increase of heavy metal mobility.\nAll anions and elements dissolved in the eluates could be related to the electrolyte contents in the battery’s electrodes. In particular, the presence of potassium hydroxide (Ni–Cd and Ni-MH batteries), lithium salts as LiPF LiBF LiAsF (Li-ion batteries) and some sulphate and chloride salts can be inferred. The tests resulted in low leached concentrations of all metals with the exception of lithium and potassium.\nThe leaching tests did not consider other anions that could be present, including phosphates, arsenates, and borates. In addition, it should be noted that the high pH values found resulted from a specific leaching test and other pH values and other metal concentrations could be found with different leaching conditions. Still, the high pH values suggest great care in handling this material, which would be highly caustic and corrosive coming into contact with water or humidity.
